title: How to choose floss colours for cross-stitch
subtitle: Reading colour keys, substituting shades, and building your own palette
excerpt: Choosing floss colours means matching a chart's colour key to the brand you have, understanding how printed colour codes translate to the thread in hand, and knowing when a close substitute is good enough and when it is not.
sourceNotes: Floss colour management practice follows standard cross-stitch convention. DMC, Anchor, and Madeira equivalence tables are published by each manufacturer.

content.text: colours means finding the thread that matches each code in the chart's colour key, then deciding whether you want the exact code or a close shade from the same brand. Most charts use DMC codes because DMC is the most widely stocked. Anchor and Madeira publish conversion tables with their own code for each DMC number.

The printed colour on a chart page or a digital chart on screen is not a reliable guide to what the finished stitches will look like. Print quality and screen calibration both affect the apparent shade. When in doubt, hold the skein against the
or linen you plan to use, not against the chart printout.

A chart colour key lists each symbol used on the chart, its code (e.g. DMC 3865), the brand name for that code (usually a descriptive name like "Winter White"), and sometimes the stitch count for that colour. The stitch count tells you roughly how much thread is used; a colour covering 500 stitches on 14-count Aida will need about one full skein.
If the exact DMC code is not available, look at the code number. DMC codes within ten to twenty numbers of each other in the same colour family are usually close in tone.

For background and fill colours (a large pale sky, a grass border), a close substitute is usually fine. For eye colours, skin tones, and fine detail areas, the exact code matters more because slight differences will be visible in a large stitched area.

For Anchor or Madeira substitution, use the conversion table the manufacturer publishes. The tables are not always exact: where two similar DMC shades map to the same Anchor code, note which of the two the table says is the closest match.
Stitch a one-square sample of any substitute colour on a scrap of the intended fabric before committing to the whole piece. Hold the swatch next to the printed chart in daylight.
Choosing colours for your own design

When designing your own colour scheme without a chart, start by picking a light, a mid, and a dark shade from the same colour family. This gives shading depth with a minimum of colours. Then add one or two accent colours from the opposite side of the colour wheel to add contrast to the palette.

items.symptom: The skein colour looks nothing like the printed chart
items.cause: Printed chart colours vary by printer and screen calibration. The printed square is a guide, not an exact match.
items.fix: Hold the skein against the actual fabric in daylight, not against the chart printout. The fabric background changes how the thread reads.

items.symptom: Two similar shades look identical under artificial light
items.cause: Tungsten and LED lighting shifts how close colours read against each other.
items.fix: Compare skeins near a window in natural light. If two shades are genuinely close in tone, stitch a small test square of each on a scrap of fabric and compare them side by side in daylight.

content.text: Once you have the colours gathered and wound onto bobbins, the next step is organising them by section of the chart before beginning. A sheet of paper with each code and its symbol, sorted by the section of the piece they appear in, saves time when switching between colours during stitching.

glossaryTerms.definition: The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.
